text: This is the minimum minute by minute monitoring data required for inclusion in the BrainIT Database and include: Heart Rate, Respiration Rate, Mean Arterial Pressure, mean ICP, SaO2 and Temperature. Data is collected from patients every minute.

text: Secondary insults such as intracranial hypertension, systemic hypotension, arterial hypotension, jugular venous desaturation, and acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) occur frequently in head injured patients despite baseline intensive care management. Secondary insult treatment covers non-surgical therapy specifically given to treat secondary insults. For example, arterial pressors may be given to treat systemic hypotension or to treat reduced cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) secondary to raised ICP. The minute by minute monitoring data allows clinicians to detect these conditions.

source: Moss et al. (2013) Trusting Intensive Care Unit (ICU) Medical Data
text: Each patient has monitoring sessions. Each timepoint in a monitoring session is associated with observations produced by sensors. Each observation measures a physiological parameter and is evaluated by a data quality assessment resulting in either a Possible Error (PoE) or Probable Error (PrE) classification. A reading outside range may be contextualised by a medical disorder (e.g. sepsis, hypertension) or recent treatment (e.g. noradrenaline), reclassifying a PrE as PoE.

source: Shaw et al. (2024) Exploration of the relationship between PbtO2 and ICP
text: Clinical management of this population is focused on minimising any secondary injury, such as ischemia or raised intracranial pressure (ICP). A variety of vital signs monitoring modalities are used concurrently in neuro-intensive care units. The currently proposed treatment protocols use a combined PbtO2 and ICP monitoring strategy with cut-offs of 20 mmHg for PbtO2 and 22 mmHg for ICP. There is a known non-linear effect of PbtO2 on cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP), which is the net pressure differential driving cerebral blood flow. Patient outcome was assessed using GOSe at 6 months.

source: Decraene et al. (2023) Decompressive craniectomy as a second/third-tier intervention in TBI
text: Uncontrollable intracranial hypertension is a major cause of death in patients with severe traumatic brain injury. One of the cornerstones of brain-protective strategies is to reduce and control intracranial pressure (ICP). First-tier treatments include head elevation, neuromuscular paralysis, analgesia, continued sedation, normocapnia and normothermia. When despite interventions ICP remained unacceptably high, decompressive craniectomy was chosen, with or without third-tier medical therapy with barbiturates (thiopental). Mean ICP, mean CPP and mean PRx were calculated. Patient outcome was assessed using the GOSe at six months.

source: Donald et al. (2012) Trigger Characteristics of EUSIG-Defined Hypotensive Events
text: Hypotension is a recognized secondary insult after traumatic brain injury (TBI). Several authors have shown that significant periods of arterial hypotension consistently relate to clinical outcome. The Edinburgh University Secondary Insult Grades (EUSIG) provides threshold values for 14 secondary insult categories. Our definition of hypotension is systolic blood pressure less than 90 mmHg or mean arterial blood pressure less than 70 mmHg for a holddown of 5 minutes. Using this definition we identified 2,081 events from 100 patients.

source: Güiza et al. (2015) Visualizing the Pressure and Time Burden of Intracranial Hypertension
text: Intracranial pressure (ICP) monitoring was introduced as a monitoring tool for severe TBI. The recommended treatment threshold for ICP-lowering therapies is 20 mmHg. An increased ICP is an independent risk factor for mortality. Data collection included baseline risk factors (age, gender, admission GCS, admission pupil reactivity), minute-by-minute ICP and mean arterial blood pressure (MAP) monitoring data, and Glasgow Outcome Score (GOS) at 6 months. Cerebrovascular pressure autoregulation is often impaired in severe TBI, and such impairment is independently associated with worse outcomes.

source: Stell et al. (2018) Automated Measurement of Adherence to TBI Guidelines
text: Using physiological and treatment information from neurological ICU data-sets, adherence to TBI guidelines on hypotension, intracranial pressure (ICP) and cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) is calculated automatically. Aggressive attempts to maintain CPP above 70 mm Hg with fluids and pressors should be avoided because of the risk of adult respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). CPP of less than 50 mm Hg should be avoided. Patients with intact pressure autoregulation tolerate higher CPP values. Ancillary monitoring of cerebral parameters includes blood flow, oxygenation, and metabolism.

text: The Edinburgh University Secondary Insult Grades (EUSIG) system classifies hypotensive events as systolic blood pressure (BPs) less than 90 mmHg or mean arterial pressure (BPm) less than 70 mmHg with a holddown period of 5 minutes. Many hypotensive events were preceded by clinical interventions such as nursing care, patient turning, or changes in sedation. Detection of a hypotensive event triggers specific therapeutic interventions including fluid resuscitation and vasopressor administration to restore adequate cerebral perfusion pressure. Several authors have shown that significant periods of arterial hypotension consistently relate to clinical outcome.

source: Decraene et al. (2023) Decompressive craniectomy as a second/third-tier intervention in TBI
text: Decompressive craniectomy (DC) was performed as a hemicraniectomy or bifrontal craniectomy. Cranioplasty was subsequently performed using the original bone flap. Therapy intensity level (TIL basic) was recorded for each patient to quantify the intensity of ICP-directed treatment. First-tier treatments include head elevation (30 degrees), neuromuscular paralysis, analgesia, and sedation. Injury mechanisms included fall (45%), road traffic accident (30%), assault (15%). In-hospital mortality was 18%. Mean ICP, CPP, and PRx were calculated before and after DC. Patient outcome was assessed using GOSe at six months.
